newsitem.title: USA: U.S. Great Plains hit by another blizzard.
newsitem.headline: U.S. Great Plains hit by another blizzard.

text.p: A blast of frigid Canadian air drove another blizzard into the Great Plains on Wednesday in a now-familiar pattern that even hardy residents complained was the worst winter they had ever experienced.

"We're in the middle of a disaster because of this weather. I've been here for 26 years and I've never seen it this tough with the snow and ice and drifts," Dr. Sam Holland, South Dakota's state veterinarian said.

The latest winter storm -- the region's ninth since the season began -- laid a fresh layer of snow and officials warned people to keep out of the deadly cold. Last week's blizzard and a bout of Arctic cold that extended as far south as Mexico was blamed for more than 30 deaths.
Winds as strong as 60 mph (95 kph) were expected to produce dangerous wind-chills of minus 80 degrees Fahrenheit (minus 62 Celsius).
Rescuers used Snowcat vehicles to rescue hundreds of motorists stranded in an unusually heavy snowfall on highways within a 50-mile (80 km) radius of Flagstaff, Arizona.

That storm moved into the Midwest on Wednesday, dropping ice, sleet and snow from Arkansas to the Ohio River valley. The two storms were expected to merge, producing snow and ice across the Eastern Seaboard.

Holland said a herd of 1,500 buffalo -- which appeared in the movie "Dances with Wolves" -- that ran off the Houk Ranch near Pierre across fences buried under snow drifts were rounded up and returned to the ranch.

Two helicopters and a band of people on snowmobiles successfully herded the animals back onto the 60,000-acre (24,000 hectare) ranch on Tuesday, where the herd is quarantined because of brucellosis infection. If spread to cattle, the disease can cause calves to be stillborn and an infection can trigger fever in humans.

The wintry weather was expected to cause huge losses to the region's cattle herd. Cattle ranching is South Dakota's highest-earning industry and thousands of animals may die from lack of feed and exposure, Holland said.
The Great Plains blizzard was further hampering efforts to re-stock store shelves, leaving some residents isolated in rural homesteads and preventing blood banks from replenishing their supply.
